title: Tier 1: the nine numbers the Dog chain starts from
body_html:
Every finder in this lane runs the same chain: nine numbers make edges, edges make shapes, shapes make the Dog. The Signature edition starts the chain from Manon's own nine numbers instead of Sobel's.

His trust-3 kernel is [[-1, 0, 1], [-3, 0, 3], [-1, 0, 1]]: the same shape as Sobel, but the middle row counts TRIPLE instead of double. His reasoning, in his words: the row you are standing on deserves the strongest vote, and three is his number for it. This is Signature-made and labeled as such - his original weighting, not a published operator, never presented as established computer-vision fact.

The demo draws the Dog test drawing on a 48-by-48 grid and runs the real 3-by-3 convolution in pure Python, no libraries. Peak response: 1050. Edge pixels above threshold: 413. Tier 2 never sees the drawing - it only ever sees these 413 edge pixels.

title: Tier 2 inventory: making the Dog from shapes
body_html:
Before any detection runs, the Dog is built as an arrangement of Tier-2 shapes on a 48-by-48 test grid. The inventory: 1 circles, 1 ellipses, 1 boxes, 3 lines.

The map below is the exact test image the finder sees - # is drawn, . is background. Everything the finder knows about a Dog lives in this map.

Each shape is drawn filled (lines are drawn thick). Edges form exactly along the outlines, which is what the Tier-2 shape finders in the next record hunt for.

title: The Tier-2 shape finders that catch each part
body_html:
Tier 2 turns edge pixels into named shapes. Each part of the Dog gets a dedicated finder: box-finder, circle-finder, ellipse-finder, line-finder.

Each finder sweeps an outline template of its shape over a small search window around the part's expected pose and scores the overlap with the real edge map. A score of 1.0 would be a perfect outline; a part counts as found at 0.40 or better.

Live scores on the test drawing - every part found: head-round 0.701; ear-flop-left 0.794; ear-flop-right 0.794; snout-box 0.736; body-blob 0.688; tail-line 0.762.

title: The shape recipe - what the Dog is made of
body_html:
A dog is a round head with ear lines flanking it, a snout box below the head, an ellipse body, and a tail line. The ears flank the head, never crown it — that arrangement is the dog rule that separates it from the cat.

Measured off the test drawing: head-round: circle, radius 6, center (24,13). ear-flop-left: line, from (17,7) to (15,14), center (16,10). ear-flop-right: line, from (31,7) to (33,14), center (32,10). snout-box: rect, 8x4 box, center (24,23). body-blob: ellipse, 20x12, center (24,34). tail-line: line, from (32,32) to (38,25), center (35,28).

Proportions are part of the recipe, not decoration: parts run from about 96 px (snout) to about 576 px (body) of bounding area. The finder expects roughly these sizes - a head the size of the body would break the arrangement gate in the next record.

title: The knowing-when rule - the decision that says "DOG FOUND"
body_html:
Knowing when the edges made the shape is a decision rule with two gates. Gate 1 - parts: every part's shape score must reach 0.40. Gate 2 - arrangement: every one of these checks must pass: 1. snout sits below head center; 2. ears flank the head, not above it; 3. body hangs below the head; 4. tail trails right of the body.

The demo runs the rule two ways. On the test Dog: FOUND, weakest part 0.688 (margin 0.287 above threshold). With the snout-box erased: FOUND (unexpected - reported honestly) - the rule genuinely depends on the parts.

Across the other twelve test drawings, this finder's full rule also fires on: Cat, Human face. Where it fires on a cousin - the cat finder also fires on the dog drawing - that is measured, not hidden: simple shape recipes overlap, and telling close cousins apart needs more evidence than outlines alone. The rule as built is reported exactly as measured.

title: The full chain, executed - nine numbers to Dog
body_html:
Here is the whole chain in one program. Tier 1 runs the nine numbers (Manon's trust-3 kernel) over the drawing and keeps the edge pixels. Tier 2 runs one shape finder per part. Tier 3 applies the knowing-when rule - part scores plus arrangement checks - and prints its verdict.

The program below is the working version of this database (find-dog-signature.py): pure Python, no libraries, no numpy. The output beneath it is the real captured stdout from the build - not a mock.

Demonstrated on synthetic test shapes. This proves the chain executes end to end on clean drawings. It does not claim detection on real photographs.

title: The finder holds - shifted, noisy, still found
body_html:
Robustness check, executed: shift the whole Dog by (+3, -2) pixels and sprinkle 40 random bright noise pixels across the grid - dirt on the lens. The finder still says FOUND.

Scores move a little (weakest part 0.698) but every part stays above 0.40 and every arrangement check passes.

What this proves: the rule tolerates small shifts and dirt. What it does not prove: rotation, occlusion, or photographs - those are outside the test.

title: Honest limits - what is proven and what is not
body_html:
Proven, by execution: on clean 48-by-48 synthetic drawings, the chain nine-numbers to edges to shapes to Dog runs end to end in pure Python, and the knowing-when rule (part scores at 0.40 plus arrangement checks) fires FOUND on the Dog - and, measured honestly, also on Cat, Human face.

Not proven: real photographs, hand-drawn variants, rotated or occluded dogs, lighting changes, or anything outside the test grid. Nothing in this database was ever run on a camera image, and nothing here claims otherwise.

Noise curve, executed (random bright pixels added): 0 noise px: 6/6 parts, 4/4 checks -> FOUND 40 noise px: 6/6 parts, 3/4 checks -> NOT FOUND 120 noise px: 6/6 parts, 4/4 checks -> FOUND 300 noise px: 6/6 parts, 4/4 checks -> FOUND.

Signature-edition content - Manon's trust-3 kernel, his part names (head-round, ear-flop-left, ear-flop-right, snout-box, body-blob, tail-line), his phrasing of the chain - is Signature-made and speculative: his originals, never presented as established computer-vision fact.
